analysis.one_liner: Bars big grocery stores and delivery apps from using shoppers' personal data to set individual prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by just two House members, has sat untouched in the Energy and Commerce Committee since its May 2026 referral, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop large grocery stores and food delivery apps from using your personal data to charge you a different, higher price than other shoppers — a practice known as dynamic pricing, which stores are starting to enable through electronic shelf labels. It would also force online grocers to tell you if an item is out of stock or priced by weight, and require delivery apps to ask before swapping out an item you ordered. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and the Labor Department would study whether electronic shelf labels cost grocery jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Grocery shoppers — especially people who order groceries online or through delivery apps — would gain protection against being charged more than their neighbors for the same food based on their data, location, or shopping habits. Grocery workers could gain indirectly if the Labor Department study on electronic shelf labels leads to scrutiny of job losses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Grocery shoppers, especially online and delivery customers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits food retailers (stores of 15,000 square feet or more) and third-party delivery providers from using any technology that sets prices based on a consumer's personal data, so the price you see can't be quietly raised for you alone.
Requires online grocers to disclose to shoppers when an item's availability has changed or when its price is determined by weight, closing common surprises in online ordering.
Requires delivery apps to get explicit approval from the customer before substituting a different grocery item for the one ordered.
Enforces all of this through the Federal Trade Commission as an unfair or deceptive practice, giving the agency its standard penalty powers over violators.

Directs the Secretary of Labor to report to Congress within a year on whether grocery stores' adoption of electronic shelf labels — the screens that make per-person pricing technically possible — affects employment.

analysis.who_pays: Large grocery chains and delivery services would bear compliance costs and lose the ability to personalize prices — a pricing tool the industry is actively building out through electronic shelf labels. Some administrative costs could trickle to consumers, and the consent-before-substitution rule could slow app operations slightly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large grocery chains and delivery apps

drawbacks.text: The exceptions are broad: a retailer can still offer personalized pricing through loyalty or reward programs as long as the consumer voluntarily enrolls or consents to share data — meaning stores could keep much of the practice by routing it through the membership cards most shoppers already carry.
It only covers food retailers of at least 15,000 square feet, leaving smaller stores and any business under that threshold free to personalize prices.
It lets retailers charge different prices based on objective costs like shipping or taxes, and allows temporary discounts to retain existing customers, so some price variation remains legal.
Requiring explicit approval before a delivery substitution could delay or complicate online orders, a real friction for shoppers who currently allow substitutions for convenience.
On the electronic shelf labels that enable the practice, the bill orders a study rather than any restriction, so the underlying technology rollout would continue while research is underway.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — no charging individual shoppers more based on their data — addresses a real and growing practice and is easy to explain. But the bill is leaky: the loyalty-program and consent exceptions leave the industry a wide legal path to the same outcome, the size threshold exempts many retailers, and it restricts nothing about the electronic shelf label hardware itself. A shopper would get real but partial protection; the strongest honest objection is that consent-based exceptions convert a ban into a paperwork rule for a practice most customers already opt into through store cards.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Josh Gottheimer introduced the bill on May 19, 2026, joined by Rep. Mike Lawler, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
That referral is the last action on record: the bill has gained only one Republican cosponsor beyond its original sponsors and has received no hearing, markup, or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, large grocery chains and delivery apps are better off: because the bill has not moved, they remain free to deploy electronic shelf labels and data-driven pricing without any of the proposed limits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Grocery chains and delivery apps, for now

for.name: Rep. Josh Gottheimer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Energy and Commerce.

for.name: Rep. Mike Lawler
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's lone Republican cosponsor at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since referral — no hearing or markup has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan — one Democrat and one Republican — but the bill has attracted no broader support from either party, with no floor votes on record.

industries.note: The bill would bar stores of 15,000 square feet or more from using shoppers' personal data to set individual prices, blocking the personalized-pricing capability the industry is building through electronic shelf labels — though loyalty-program exceptions would preserve much of the practice.

Delivery providers would face the same data-pricing ban plus a new requirement to get explicit customer approval before substituting items, adding operational friction and limiting data-driven pricing.

The bill does not restrict the digital shelf-label hardware that enables per-shopper pricing; it only orders a study of the labels' effect on grocery employment, so sales to grocery chains could continue.

analysis.trajectory: With two sponsors, no cosponsor growth, and no committee action months after referral, the bill follows the pattern of most House bills: it will likely die quietly in the Energy and Commerce Committee when the Congress ends unless its provisions get attached to a larger consumer-protection package.
